claims.text: Partial short-range ordering is the primary factor governing the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys during high-temperature service.
Partial short-range ordering is the primary factor governing the chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys during high-temperature service.
Short-range elemental clustering or partial ordering restricts defect mobility.
Short-range elemental clustering or partial ordering restricts grain-boundary mobility.
Interactions among multiple principal elements create energetically favorable local configurations.
The energetically favorable local configurations reduce grain-boundary energies.
The local configurations suppress diffusion-driven segregation at elevated temperatures.
Reducing boundary energy and suppressing diffusion-driven segregation prevent grain coarsening and phase separation.
At the same nominal composition and initial grain size, short-range-ordered samples will undergo less grain growth than chemically randomized samples.
At the same nominal composition and initial grain size, short-range-ordered samples will exhibit less elemental segregation than chemically randomized samples.
Short-range-ordered samples will remain a stable single phase after multiple high-temperature cycles.
The prediction applies primarily to near-equiatomic alloys with grain sizes below approximately 50 nm at temperatures up to approximately 1200 °C.
Above approximately 1200 °C or in strongly off-equiatomic compositions, competing enthalpic effects and interfacial instabilities may dominate stability.
Local compositional fluctuations or interfacial effects may obscure the influence of short-range ordering.
Exposure beyond the proposed test duration may produce additional phase transitions.
Using high vacuum or an inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation during thermal cycling.
